work: Enarratio in Epistolam B. Pauli ad Ephesios
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: EXPOSITIO PRIMI CAPITULI : PAULUS APOSTOLUS JESU CHRISTI PER VOLUNTATEM DEI.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, by the will of God.

paras.t: PAULUS apostolus Jesu Christi per voluntatem Dei, id est a divina voluntate ad apostolatum efficienter promotus, scribit sanctis omnibus, id est firmis et dignis Christi fidelibus, qui sunt Ephesi, id est, in urbe sic dicta commorantur, et, pro id est, fidelibus qui sunt in Christo Jesu per fidem et caritatem, sicut membra in capite. Vel, per sanctos intelligit prælatos et perfectiores; per fideles vero, imperfectiores ac subditos. Gratia vobis detur et pax a Deo Patre nostro, et Domino Jesu Christo.
paras.en: [[1:1|Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, by the will of God|PAULUS apostolus Jesu Christi per voluntatem Dei]], that is, effectively promoted to the apostleship by the divine will, writes [[1:1|to all the saints|sanctis omnibus]], that is, to the steadfast and worthy faithful of Christ, [[1:1|who are at Ephesus|qui sunt Ephesi]], that is, who dwell in the city so called, [[1:1|and|et]] (put for *that is*) [[1:1|to the faithful|fidelibus]] who are [[1:1|in Christ Jesus|in Christo Jesu]] through faith and charity, as members in the head. Or, by the saints he understands the prelates and the more perfect; by the faithful, the less perfect and the subjects. [[1:2|Grace be to you|Gratia vobis]] be given [[1:2|and peace, from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ|et pax a Deo Patre nostro, et Domino Jesu Christo]][[Gal 1:3||]].

paras.t: Salutatione præmissa, a gratiarum actione orditur, et ait: Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Omnia hæc jam prædicta verba, in præcedentium exordiis epistolarum scripta atque exposita sunt: idcirco pertranseo. Qui Deus et Pater noster, benedixit nos, id est, benedictos et gratiosos nos fecit, dando nobis munera cœlestium gratiarum, sicut subjungitur: in omni benedictione spirituali, id est in omni dono gratiæ liberaliter dato, nostroque cordi infuso, ita ut benedictio ista sit causa formalis per quam a Deo effective benedicti sumus. Frequenter autem accipitur in Scripturis benedictio pro dono liberali: sicut quum Abigail ait ad David, Accipe benedictionem quam attulit famula tua. Benedixit itaque nos omni benedictione, saltem in genere: et hoc, in cœlestibus bonis seu gratiis; vel ad hoc, ut ad cœlestia regna perveniamus; vel, Omni benedictione habenda perfecte in cœlestibus mansionibus; in Christo Jesu, id est merito Christi, sive per Christum tanquam per mediatorem.
paras.en: The greeting set first, he begins with thanksgiving, and says: [[1:3|Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ|Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Jesu Christi]][[2 Cor 1:3||]]. All these words have already been written and expounded in the openings of the preceding epistles; therefore I pass over them. [[1:3|who|Qui]], God and our Father, [[1:3|hath blessed us|benedixit nos]], that is, made us blessed and gracious, giving us the gifts of heavenly graces, as is added: [[1:3|with spiritual blessings|in omni benedictione spirituali]] [literally “in every spiritual blessing”], that is, in every gift of grace freely given and poured into our heart, so that this blessing is the formal cause by which we are effectively blessed by God. Now in the Scriptures *blessing* is often taken for a free gift: as when Abigail says to David, [[1 Kings 25:27|receive this blessing, which thy handmaid|Accipe benedictionem quam attulit famula tua]] [the Douay-Rheims reads “this present” for *benedictionem*]. So he has blessed us with every blessing, at least in kind; and this [[1:3|in heavenly places|in cœlestibus]], goods or graces; or to this end, that we may come to the heavenly kingdoms; or, with every blessing to be had perfectly in the heavenly mansions; [[1:3|in Christ|in Christo]] Jesus, that is, by the merit of Christ, or through Christ as through a mediator.

paras.t: Sicut elegit nos, id est, præ aliis multis seu reprobis ad æternam beatitudinem præordinavit, in ipso, id est in Christo, seu per Christum: ita ut Pater et Christus seu Filius, imo et cum eis Spiritus Sanctus, sint unus elector, sicut unus creator. Unde Christus testatur: Ego scio quos elegerim; et rursus, Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos. Elegit ergo nos in ipso ante mundi constitutionem, id est ab æterno: quæ electio ex dilectione processit. Potest quoque sic accipi, ut Pater dicatur nos elegisse in Christo ante mundi constitutionem, quoniam ab æterno disposuit per Christi incarnationem ac passionem impendere nobis suæ æternæ electionis effectum, id est veram salutem. Ut essemus sancti, id est puri in anima, et immaculati in opere, in conspectu ejus, id est coram Deo, videlicet vere, seu divino judicio, non tantum humano, in caritate, quæ est vita decorque animæ, id est per actum caritatis interiorem, sine quo nihil est meritorium. Unde per caritatem efficimur sancti in affectu, et immaculati in effectu.
paras.en: [[1:4|As he chose us|Sicut elegit nos]], that is, foreordained us to eternal beatitude before many others, the reprobate, [[1:4|in him|in ipso]], that is, in Christ, or through Christ: so that the Father and Christ, or the Son, and indeed with them the Holy Ghost, are one chooser, as they are one creator. Hence Christ testifies: [[John 13:18|I know whom I have chosen|Ego scio quos elegerim]]; and again, [[John 15:16|You have not chosen me: but I have chosen you|Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos]] [the margin's second note is illegible; the words are John 15:16]. So he chose us in him [[1:4|before the foundation of the world|ante mundi constitutionem]], that is, from eternity: and this election proceeded from love. It can also be taken thus, that the Father is said to have chosen us in Christ before the foundation of the world because from eternity he disposed to bestow on us, through Christ's incarnation and passion, the effect of his eternal election, that is, true salvation. [[1:4|that we should be holy|Ut essemus sancti]], that is, pure in soul, [[1:4|and unspotted|et immaculati]] in work, [[1:4|in his sight|in conspectu ejus]], that is, before God, namely truly, by divine judgment, not by human only, [[1:4|in charity|in caritate]], which is the life and beauty of the soul, that is, through the interior act of charity, without which nothing is meritorious[[1 Cor 13:1||]]. Hence through charity we are made holy in affection and unspotted in effect.

paras.t: Qui Pater prædestinavit, id est, ad vitam æternam in sua dispositione præmisit seu præordinavit, nos in adoptionem filiorum, id est ad hoc, ut bona gratiæ quæ filiis adoptivis præstantur, nobis donentur. Quod autem subjungitur, per Jesum Christum, referri potest vel ad verbum, Prædestinavit, vel ad nomen, Filiorum, quia per Filium dicimur prædestinati, sicut electi. Per Filium quoque adoptio filialis nobis confertur: dedit enim nobis potestatem filios Dei fieri. Sic autem prædestinavit nos in ipsum, id est ad imitationem filiationis naturalis quæ convenit Christo, cujus similitudo est filiatio adoptiva; vel, In ipsum, id est, ut veniamus ad gloriam Christi, et ejus efficiamur coheredes. Prædestinavit insuper secundum propositum, id est æternum decretum, voluntatis suæ, qua omnia liberrime agit, id est, secundum voluntatem suam divinam, omnia juste agentem ac proponentem: quæ utique est prima causa prædestinationis;
paras.en: [[1:5|Who|Qui]], the Father, [[1:5|hath predestinated|prædestinavit]], that is, sent beforehand or foreordained in his disposition to eternal life, [[1:5|us unto the adoption of children|nos in adoptionem filiorum]], that is, to this end, that the goods of grace bestowed on adopted children may be given to us. What is added, [[1:5|through Jesus Christ|per Jesum Christum]], may be referred either to the verb *predestinated* or to the noun *children*, since we are said to be predestinated through the Son, as we are chosen. Through the Son also filial adoption is conferred on us: for he gave us [[John 1:12|power to be made the sons of God|potestatem filios Dei fieri]]. And so he predestinated us [[1:5|unto himself|in ipsum]], that is, to the imitation of the natural sonship that belongs to Christ, of which adoptive sonship is a likeness; or, *unto him*, that is, that we may come to the glory of Christ and be made his coheirs. Moreover he predestinated [[1:5|according to the purpose|secundum propositum]], that is, the eternal decree, [[1:5|of his will|voluntatis suæ]], by which he does all things most freely, that is, according to his divine will, which does and purposes all things justly: and this indeed is the first cause of predestination;

paras.t: in laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ, id est, ut laudemus magnificentiam gratiæ suæ gratum facientis, per quam adoptio filiorum Dei nunc inchoatur, quæ in patria per lumen gloriæ consummatur; in qua gratia gratum faciente, id est per quam, formaliter gratificavit, id est, sibi acceptos ac gratos nos fecit, in dilecto Filio suo, id est per Christum mediatorem Dei et hominum, scilicet merito Christi, et per omnia quæ Christus pro nostra salute assumpsit, fecit ac pertulit.
paras.en: [[1:6|Unto the praise of the glory of his grace|in laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ]], that is, that we may praise the magnificence of his sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God], by which the adoption of the sons of God is now begun, which in our heavenly fatherland is consummated by the light of glory; [[1:6|in which|in qua]] sanctifying grace, that is, by which, formally, [[1:6|he hath graced|gratificavit]], that is, made [[1:6|us|nos]] accepted and pleasing to himself, [[1:6|in his beloved son|in dilecto Filio suo]], that is, through Christ, [[1 Tim 2:5|mediator of God and men|mediator Dei et hominum]], namely by the merit of Christ and by all that Christ took on, did and suffered for our salvation.

paras.t: In quo Filio Dei dilecto habemus redemptionem a jure et jugo diaboli, per sanguinem ejus, id est merito effusionis sui pretiosissimi sanguinis: juxta illud, Qui dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo. Ideo subditur: remissionem peccatorum, id est, redemptio ista est vitiorum nostrorum solutio: quæ facta est secundum divitias, id est plenitudinem, gratiæ ejus, videlicet Christi, qui gratiose et pie nos liberavit. Unde per evangelistam Joannem dicitur: Gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est; et de plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus, et gratiam pro gratia.
paras.en: [[1:7|In whom|In quo]], the beloved Son of God, [[1:7|we have redemption|habemus redemptionem]] from the right and yoke of the devil, [[1:7|through his blood|per sanguinem ejus]], that is, by the merit of the shedding of his most precious blood: according to that saying, [[Apoc 1:5|who hath loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood|Qui dilexit nos, et lavit nos a peccatis nostris in sanguine suo]]. Therefore is added: [[1:7|the remission of sins|remissionem peccatorum]], that is, this redemption is the loosing of our sins: which was done [[1:7|according to the riches|secundum divitias]], that is, the fulness, [[1:7|of his, grace|gratiæ ejus]], namely of Christ, who graciously and lovingly set us free. Hence it is said by John the evangelist: [[John 1:17|grace and truth came by Jesus Christ|Gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est]]; and [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received: and grace for grace|de plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus, et gratiam pro gratia]].

paras.t: Quæ gratia superabundavit in nobis apostolis, id est, copiosissime nobis infusa est, quippe qui primitias Spiritus Sancti accepimus, in omni sapientia, id est divinorum notitia omni, quantum ad sacram spectat Scripturam, quam plene cognoscimus, et prudentia, id est temporalium et humanarum rerum agnitione.
paras.en: [[1:8|Which|Quæ]] grace [[1:8|hath superabounded in us|superabundavit in nobis]] apostles, that is, was most copiously poured into us, seeing that we have received [[Rom 8:23|the firstfruits of the Spirit|primitias Spiritus]], [[1:8|in all wisdom|in omni sapientia]], that is, in all knowledge of divine things as regards holy Scripture, which we know fully, [[1:8|and prudence|et prudentia]], that is, in the knowledge of temporal and human things.

paras.t: Hæc enim nobis per gratiam Spiritus Sancti collata sunt, ut notum faceret nobis sacramentum, id est secretum, voluntatis suæ, seu voluntatem suam secretam, aliis occultatam, vel incarnationis Christi mysterium, seu divinæ mentis consilium circa humani generis redemptionem, secundum beneplacitum ejus, id est secundum quod sibi pie complacuit, quod proposuit in eo, id est, cujus placiti exsecutionem constituit et implevit in Christo. Quid autem, et quando factum sit hoc, subditur: in dispensatione plenitudinis temporum, id est adveniente tempore divinitus præordinato et dispensato, videlicet tempore gratiæ, de quo alibi dictum est: Ecce jam venit plenitudo temporis; instaurare omnia in Christo, id est per Christi mysteria reformare, quæ in cœlis, id est ordines angelorum, supplendo ruinas eorum, et quæ in terra sunt, id est genus humanum, in ipso, id est eos qui in Christo electi sunt, qui soli effectum divinæ liberationis finaliter sortiuntur.
paras.en: For these things were bestowed on us through the grace of the Holy Ghost, [[1:9|That he might make known unto us the mystery|ut notum faceret nobis sacramentum]], that is, the secret, [[1:9|of his will|voluntatis suæ]], or his secret will, hidden from others, or the mystery of Christ's incarnation, or the counsel of the divine mind concerning the redemption of mankind, [[1:9|according to his good pleasure|secundum beneplacitum ejus]], that is, according to what lovingly pleased him, [[1:9|which he hath purposed in him|quod proposuit in eo]], that is, the carrying out of which good pleasure he appointed and fulfilled in Christ. What this is, and when it was done, is added: [[1:10|In the dispensation of the fulness of times|in dispensatione plenitudinis temporum]], that is, when the time divinely foreordained and dispensed had come, namely the time of grace, of which it is said elsewhere: Behold, now the fulness of time has come[[Gal 4:4||]] [Denis's wording is loose; Gal 4:4 reads “when the fulness of the time was come”]; [[1:10|to re-establish all things in Christ|instaurare omnia in Christo]], that is, to reform through the mysteries of Christ the things [[1:10|that are in heaven|quæ in cœlis]], that is, the orders of angels, by filling up their ruins, [[1:10|and on earth|et quæ in terra sunt]], that is, mankind, [[1:10|in him|in ipso]], that is, those who are chosen in Christ, who alone finally obtain the effect of the divine deliverance.

paras.t: In quo, id est, per quem Christum, et nos apostoli, sicut et ceteri electi, sorte, id est divina electione, vocati sumus ad fidem et gratiam salutarem. Dicitur autem sors, divina electio, quia utrumque est Dei, non hominis; et sicut electio non accipit personam, ita nec sors. Propter quod ait Scriptura: Sortes mittuntur in sinum, sed a Domino temperantur. Prædestinati, id est ad æternam beatitudinem præordinati, secundum propositum ejus, id est secundum æternam incommutabilis ejus decreti dispositionem, qui omnia operatur per se ipsum vel causas secundas, secundum consilium voluntatis suæ, id est secundum certissimam rationem suæ voluntati consonam atque placentem. Nil enim operatur ad extra de necessitate aut casu, sed sapienter ac libere universa producit, juxta illud: Omnia in sapientia fecisti; et, Omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit.
paras.en: [[1:11|In whom|In quo]], that is, through which Christ, [[1:11|we also|et nos]] apostles, as also the other elect, [[1:11|by lot|sorte]], that is, by divine election, [[1:11|are called|vocati sumus]] to faith and saving grace. Divine election is called a *lot* because both are of God, not of man; and as election is no respecter of persons, neither is the lot. Wherefore Scripture says: [[Prov 16:33|Lots are cast into the lap, but they are disposed of by the Lord|Sortes mittuntur in sinum, sed a Domino temperantur]]. [[1:11|being predestinated|Prædestinati]], that is, foreordained to eternal beatitude, [[1:11|according to the purpose of him|secundum propositum ejus]], that is, according to the eternal disposition of his unchangeable decree, [[1:11|who worketh all things|qui omnia operatur]] by himself or by second causes, [[1:11|according to the counsel of his will|secundum consilium voluntatis suæ]], that is, according to a most certain reason, in accord with his will and pleasing to it. For he works nothing outside himself of necessity or by chance, but produces all things wisely and freely, according to that: [[Ps 103:24|thou hast made all things in wisdom|Omnia in sapientia fecisti]]; and, [[Ps 134:6|Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done|Omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit]].

paras.t: Ut simus in laudem gloriæ ejus, id est, in nobis Deus glorificetur, qui tantam gratiam nobis sine meritis nostris ineffabili pietate largitus est: ex cujus beneficii consideratione nos ipsi aliique fideles in laudem et gloriam Dei erumpere debemus; nos qui ante speravimus in Christo, id est nos apostoli, qui ante eos qui per nostram prædicationem conversi sunt, Christo per fidem et spem inhæsimus.
paras.en: [[1:12|That we may be unto the praise of his glory|Ut simus in laudem gloriæ ejus]], that is, that God may be glorified in us, who with unspeakable kindness has bestowed so great a grace on us without our merits: from the consideration of which benefit we ourselves and the other faithful ought to break out in the praise and glory of God; [[1:12|we who before hoped in Christ|nos qui ante speravimus in Christo]], that is, we apostles, who before those converted by our preaching clung to Christ by faith and hope.

paras.t: In quo Christo, id est cujus ordinatione et adjutorio, et vos, Ephesii, quum audissetis, non solum auribus corporis, sed etiam cordis, verbum veritatis, scilicet Evangelium salutis vestræ, id est doctrinam Christi annuntiantem hominum liberationem, in cujus doctrinæ observatione salus vestra consistit. In quo et credentes, id est, cui Evangelio fidem adhibentes, signati estis, id est inter electos computati, et a perversis distincti certis divinæ prædestinationis indiciis: quorum unum est illud. Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit; et, Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud; Spiritu promissionis Sancto, id est virtute et operatione Spiritus Sancti electis promissi: juxta illud in Luca, Ego mittam promissum Patris mei in vos. Vel, Spiritus Sanctus dicitur Spiritus promissionis, quia promittit vitam æternam.
paras.en: [[1:13|In whom|In quo]], Christ, that is, by whose ordinance and help, [[1:13|you also|et vos]], Ephesians, [[1:13|after you had heard|quum audissetis]], not only with the ears of the body but also of the heart, [[1:13|the word of truth|verbum veritatis]], namely [[1:13|the gospel of your salvation|Evangelium salutis vestræ]], that is, the doctrine of Christ announcing the deliverance of men, in the keeping of which doctrine your salvation consists. [[1:13|in whom also believing|In quo et credentes]], that is, giving faith to which Gospel, [[1:13|you were signed|signati estis]], that is, counted among the elect and distinguished from the perverse by sure signs of divine predestination: one of which is this: [[John 8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God|Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]]; and, [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]; [[1:13|with the holy Spirit of promise|Spiritu promissionis Sancto]], that is, by the power and working of the Holy Ghost promised to the elect: according to that in Luke, [[Luke 24:49|I send the promise of my Father upon you|Ego mittam promissum Patris mei in vos]]. Or, the Holy Ghost is called the Spirit of promise because he promises eternal life.

paras.t: Qui Spiritus Sanctus est pignus hereditatis nostræ, id est arrha futuræ felicitatis: quia per ejus inhabitationem, inspirationem, consolationem ac cetera dona, certificamur de beatitudine subsequente. Ex perceptione quippe præsentium munerum, certa fit exspectatio futurorum.
paras.en: [[1:14|Who|Qui]], the Holy Ghost, [[1:14|is the pledge of our inheritance|est pignus hereditatis nostræ]], that is, the earnest [*arrha*, a down payment] of future happiness: for by his indwelling, inspiration, consolation and other gifts we are made sure of the beatitude to follow. For from the receiving of present gifts the expectation of future ones becomes certain.

paras.t: Dicitur ergo Spiritus Sanctus pignus hereditatis quam habituri sumus in patria, quia per modum pignoris interim nobis confertur. Pignus enim est loco rei non habitæ, estque ejusdem valoris cum ea. Deus autem est nostra felicitas atque hereditas objectalis, quamvis fruitio Dei sit hereditas nostra felicitasque formalis. Hanc autem hereditatem nondum habemus in re, sed Spiritus Sanctus quem interim habemus per suam gratiosam inhabitationem, est ejusdem valoris cum ea: imo ipse realiter idem cum ea est, sed diverso habetur modo in via et in patria: ideo modo vocatur pignus, in patria autem vocatur hereditas. Verumtamen, ut in glossa quoque Augustini testantur citata verba, convenientius dicitur Spiritus Sanctus arrha quam pignus: quoniam pignus aufertur quum promissum vel debitum solvitur; arrha vero, quum sit pars pretii, non aufertur, sed completur quum solutio agitur. Quoniam ergo in perceptione futuræ atque cœlestis hereditatis Spiritus Sanctus non aufertur electis, sed plenius datur, idcirco aptius nuncupatur arrha quam pignus. Nihilo minus, quoniam Spiritus Sanctus dicitur nobis dari per dona sua, id est propter hoc quod dona sua nobis præstantur, et aliqua dona sua propter imperfectionem inclusam non manent in patria, ut fides et spes; ideo quantum ad hæc dona, Spiritus Sanctus rationem pignoris habet. Sic enim aufertur quantum ad modum, venientibus dotibus quæ fidei et spei succedunt; quantum vero ad dona quæ manent et perficiuntur in patria, qualia sunt, caritas, sapientia, timor filialis, Spiritus Sanctus proprie dictus est arrha.
paras.en: The Holy Ghost, then, is called the pledge of the inheritance we shall have in our fatherland, because meanwhile he is given us after the manner of a pledge. For a pledge stands in place of a thing not yet had, and is of the same value with it. Now God is our objective happiness and inheritance, though the enjoyment of God is our formal inheritance and happiness. This inheritance we do not yet have in reality; but the Holy Ghost, whom meanwhile we have by his gracious indwelling, is of the same value with it: indeed he is really the same as it, but is had in a different way on the way and in the fatherland: therefore now he is called a pledge, but in the fatherland he is called the inheritance. Yet, as the words of Augustine cited in the Gloss also testify, the Holy Ghost is more fittingly called an earnest than a pledge: for a pledge is taken back when the promise or debt is paid; but an earnest, being part of the price, is not taken back, but completed when payment is made. Since, then, in receiving the future heavenly inheritance the Holy Ghost is not taken away from the elect but given more fully, he is more aptly named an earnest than a pledge. Nevertheless, since the Holy Ghost is said to be given us through his gifts, that is, because his gifts are bestowed on us, and some of his gifts, by reason of the imperfection they contain, do not remain in the fatherland, as faith and hope[[1 Cor 13:8||]]; therefore as regards these gifts the Holy Ghost has the character of a pledge. For thus he is taken away as to mode, when the endowments [*dotes*, the gifts of the glorified] come that succeed faith and hope; but as regards the gifts that remain and are perfected in the fatherland, such as charity, wisdom, filial fear, the Holy Ghost is properly called an earnest.

paras.t: In redemptionem acquisitionis, id est in liberationem salvificam, per quam adipiscimur vitam æternam, videlicet ut a jugo peccati dæmonumque per gratiam Spiritus Sancti erepti, salutem acquiramus perpetuam: de qua ait Petrus, Vos genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis; in laudem gloriæ ejus, id est ad præconium divinæ beatitudinis ac majestatis, puta ad hoc ut divinæ naturæ beatitudinem ac majestatem grata mente laudemus. Omnia enim propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus.
paras.en: [[1:14|unto the redemption of acquisition|In redemptionem acquisitionis]], that is, unto the saving deliverance by which we obtain eternal life, namely that, rescued by the grace of the Holy Ghost from the yoke of sin and of the demons, we may acquire everlasting salvation: of which Peter says, [[1 Pet 2:9|you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people|Vos genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis]]; [[1:14|unto the praise of his glory|in laudem gloriæ ejus]], that is, to the proclaiming of the divine beatitude and majesty, namely that we may praise with grateful mind the beatitude and majesty of the divine nature. For [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made all things for himself|Omnia enim propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus]].

paras.t: Denique littera ista, quantum ad tenorem verborum, nonnihil truncata est. Unde supplere oportet: ut quum dicitur, In quo et credentes, fiat puncti distinctio; sicque facile elicitur sensus perfectus.
paras.en: Lastly, this text is somewhat truncated as regards the run of the words. Hence it must be supplied: so that where it says, [[1:13|in whom also believing|In quo et credentes]], a stop is made; and thus the complete sense is easily drawn out.

paras.t: Et quia bonus prælatus, imo et quilibet proximus, de salute alterius ex vera caritate lætari, et Domino gratias agere debet, subjecit Apostolus: Propterea et ego audiens a narrantibus, vel etiam ab interna locutione Spiritus Sancti, fidem vestram quæ est in Christo Jesu, id est puram, sanctam, christianam atque catholicam, et dilectionem habitualem et actualem quam ostenditis in omnes sanctos, id est in universos veraciter christianos, quibus in spiritualibus ac temporalibus benefacitis, prout casus occurrit facultasque suppetit; non cesso, congruentibus horis, gratias agens Deo pro vobis, id est propter beneficia vobis impensa, memoriam vestri faciens, id est vestri recordans, in orationibus meis, quibus pro vestro profectu oro:
paras.en: And since a good prelate, and indeed any neighbour, ought out of true charity to rejoice at another's salvation and give thanks to the Lord, the Apostle added: [[1:15|Wherefore, I also, hearing|Propterea et ego audiens]] from those who told it, or also from the inward speaking of the Holy Ghost, [[1:15|of your faith that is in|fidem vestram quæ est in]] Christ Jesus, that is, pure, holy, Christian and catholic, [[1:15|and of your love|et dilectionem]], habitual and actual, which you show [[1:15|towards all the saints|in omnes sanctos]], that is, towards all true Christians, to whom you do good in spiritual and temporal things as occasion arises and means allow; [[1:16|Cease not|non cesso]], at fitting hours, [[1:16|to give thanks|gratias agens]] to God [[1:16|for you|pro vobis]], that is, for the benefits bestowed on you, [[1:16|making commemoration of you|memoriam vestri faciens]], that is, remembering you, [[1:16|in my prayers|in orationibus meis]], in which I pray for your progress:

paras.t: Ut Deus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, id est verus Deus, qui est Deus Christi prout homo. Sic enim quælibet divina Persona, totaque simul superbeatissima Trinitas, Deus est Christi. Qui Deus est Pater gloriæ, id est fons et origo omnis sanctæ lætitiæ; vel, Pater gloriæ, id est majestatis altissimæ; det vobis spiritum, id est donum, sapientiæ, quæ est unum ac summum septem donorum Spiritus Sancti; vel, Spiritum sapientiæ, id est Spiritum Sanctum, datorem sapientiæ habitualis; et revelationis actualis, id est illuminationis ex habitu sapientiæ et motione Spiritus Sancti procedentis. Non enim sufficit nobis gratia aut sapientia habitualis; sed requiritur insuper actualis motio Spiritus Sancti, excitantis habitum ipsum in actum: cujus motionis efficitur anima cito capax per habitualia septem dona Spiritus Sancti, quemadmodum capax est motionis propriæ rationis per habitus virtutum.
paras.en: [[1:17|That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ|Ut Deus Domini nostri Jesu Christi]], that is, the true God, who is the God of Christ as man. For thus each divine Person, and the whole most blessed Trinity together, is the God of Christ. Which God is [[1:17|the Father of glory|Pater gloriæ]], that is, the fount and origin of all holy joy; or, *Father of glory*, that is, of the highest majesty; [[1:17|may give unto you the spirit|det vobis spiritum]], that is, the gift, [[1:17|of wisdom|sapientiæ]], which is one, and the highest, of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]; or, *the spirit of wisdom*, that is, the Holy Ghost, giver of habitual wisdom; [[1:17|and of revelation|et revelationis]], actual, that is, of illumination proceeding from the habit of wisdom and the motion of the Holy Ghost. For habitual grace or wisdom does not suffice us; but there is required besides the actual motion of the Holy Ghost, stirring the habit itself into act: of which motion the soul is made readily receptive by the seven habitual gifts of the Holy Ghost, as it is receptive of the motion of its own reason by the habits of the virtues.

paras.t: Det itaque vobis spiritum sapientiæ in agnitione ejus, id est ad contemplandum Deum: quod est, illuminatos habere oculos cordis vestri, id est habere intellectum speculativum ac practicum divinitus illustratum, ut sciatis, et sciendo juste vivatis: sciatis, inquam, quæ sit spes vocationis vestræ, id est bonum speratum, sive felicitas ad quam divinitus invitamur, et quæ divitiæ, id est spirituales opulentiæ seu plenitudines copiosæ, gloriæ hereditatis ejus, id est gloriosæ felicitatis Dei, quam exhibet in Sanctis in patria. Beatitudo enim est status omnium bonorum aggregatione perfectus, juxta Boetium. Unde, quamvis beatitudo Dei in se ipso sit simplicissima, beatitudo quoque quam electis infundit, secundum suam essentiam simplex sit, scilicet visio Dei, quæ est tota merces; dicimus tamen, secundum nostræ intelligentiæ modum, quod in Deo sit omnium bonorum copiosissima opulentia atque ditissima plenitudo. Beatitudini autem creatæ quæ communicatur Beatis, multa junguntur perficientia eam, videlicet dilectio, delectatio, etc., quæ dicuntur divitiæ gloriosæ hereditatis seu beatitudinis nobis promissæ. Orat ergo Apostolus ut beatitudinis hujus divitias magis perfecte cognoscant.
paras.en: May he therefore give you the spirit of wisdom [[1:17|in the knowledge of him|in agnitione ejus]], that is, for contemplating God: which is to have [[1:18|The eyes of your heart enlightened|illuminatos oculos cordis vestri]], that is, to have the speculative and practical intellect divinely enlightened, [[1:18|that you may know|ut sciatis]], and knowing may live justly: that you may know, I say, [[1:18|what the hope is of his calling|quæ sit spes vocationis]] [the printed text has *vestræ*, “your”, with a margin note *ejus*, “his”], that is, the good hoped for, or the happiness to which we are divinely invited, [[1:18|and what are the riches|et quæ divitiæ]], that is, the spiritual opulence or copious fulness, [[1:18|of the glory of his inheritance|gloriæ hereditatis ejus]], that is, of the glorious happiness of God, which he shows [[1:18|in the saints|in Sanctis]] in the fatherland. For beatitude is a state made perfect by the gathering of all goods, according to Boethius. Hence, although God's beatitude in himself is most simple, and the beatitude he pours into the elect is also simple in its essence, namely the vision of God, which is the whole reward, we nevertheless say, according to the mode of our understanding, that in God there is a most copious opulence and richest fulness of all goods. And to the created beatitude communicated to the blessed many things are joined that perfect it, namely love, delight, etc., which are called the riches of the glorious inheritance or beatitude promised us. The Apostle therefore prays that they may know the riches of this beatitude more perfectly.

paras.t: Sciatis præterea et quæ sit supereminens magnitudo, id est incomparabilis sublimitas, summaque gratia, virtutis ejus in nos, id est divinæ potestatis gratiam tantam cordibus nostris infundentis, qui credidimus in Christum, atque primitias Spiritus Sancti recepimus, secundum operationem potentiæ virtutis ejus, id est secundum efficaciam ejus divinæ potentiæ: quæ virtus vocatur, quum sit potestas consummata atque perfecta. Realiter tamen idem sunt, præsertim in Deo, potentia activa et virtus, quamvis potentia, secundum quosdam, dicat potentiam absolute, virtus autem complementum potentiæ.
paras.en: May you know moreover [[1:19|And what is the exceeding greatness|et quæ sit supereminens magnitudo]], that is, the incomparable sublimity and highest grace, [[1:19|of his power towards us|virtutis ejus in nos]], that is, of the divine power pouring so great a grace into our hearts, [[1:19|who believe|qui credimus]] in Christ [Denis reads *credidimus*, “who have believed”], and have received the firstfruits of the Holy Ghost[[Rom 8:23||]], [[1:19|according to the operation of the might of his power|secundum operationem potentiæ virtutis ejus]], that is, according to the efficacy of his divine might: which is called *virtue* [*virtus*, translated “power”], since it is power consummated and perfect. Yet in reality active power and virtue are the same, especially in God, though *power*, according to some, signifies power simply, and *virtue* the completion of power.

paras.t: Quam virtutem operatus est, id est, operando monstravit, in Christo mortuo ac sepulto, suscitans illum a mortuis tertio die, et constituens, id est, firmiter ponens eum, ad dexteram suam, id est in potioribus bonis suis, videlicet in summo honore, dignitate et gloria, in cœlestibus, id est in cœlo empyreo: supra omnem Principatum, id est angelos de summo seu tertio choro infimæ hierarchiæ, et Potestatem, id est angelos de infimo choro secundæ hierarchiæ, et Virtutem, id est angelos de medio choro ejusdem hierarchiæ, et Dominationem, id est angelos de summo ordine hierarchiæ secundæ. In hac auctoritate fundat se beatissimus theologorum princeps Dionysius, ponens Principatus in infima hierarchia. Constituit quoque eum in die ascensionis, quoad naturam assumptam, et supra omne nomen, id est ultra omne ens nominatum aut nominabile, quod nominatur, id est, exprimitur, scitur, vel esse perhibetur, non solum in hoc sæculo variabili, sed etiam in futuro, id est, in patria nominabitur aut scietur: id est, ultra omnem creaturam terrestrem et cœlestem, corporalem ac spiritualem, sublimavit Christum quoad humanitatem assumptam; imo sola humanitas Christi, propter unionem suam personalem cum Verbo, præstantior est toto universo simul accepto.
paras.en: [[1:20|Which|Quam]] power [[1:20|he wrought|operatus est]], that is, showed by working, [[1:20|in Christ|in Christo]] dead and buried, [[1:20|raising him up from the dead|suscitans illum a mortuis]] on the third day, [[1:20|and setting|et constituens]], that is, firmly placing him, [[1:20|on his right hand|ad dexteram suam]], that is, in his better goods, namely in the highest honour, dignity and glory, [[1:20|in the heavenly places|in cælestibus]], that is, in the empyrean heaven: [[1:21|Above all principality|supra omnem Principatum]], that is, the angels of the highest or third choir of the lowest hierarchy, [[1:21|and power|et Potestatem]], that is, the angels of the lowest choir of the second hierarchy, [[1:21|and virtue|et Virtutem]], that is, the angels of the middle choir of the same hierarchy, [[1:21|and dominion|et Dominationem]], that is, the angels of the highest order of the second hierarchy. On this authority the most blessed prince of theologians, Dionysius, bases himself in placing the Principalities in the lowest hierarchy. He set him also on the day of the ascension, as to the assumed nature, [[1:21|and every name|et omne nomen]], that is, beyond every being named or nameable, [[1:21|that is named|quod nominatur]], that is, expressed, known, or said to be, [[1:21|not only in this world|non solum in hoc sæculo]], changeable, [[1:21|but also in that which is to come|sed etiam in futuro]], that is, will be named or known in the fatherland: that is, beyond every creature, earthly and heavenly, bodily and spiritual, he exalted Christ as to his assumed humanity; indeed the humanity of Christ alone, because of its personal union with the Word, is more excellent than the whole universe taken together.

paras.t: Et omnia subjecit sub pedibus ejus, id est, universa creata Christi potestati atque imperio, imo et inferiori ejus naturæ (quæ nomine pedum intelligi potest), Deus Pater plenissime subdidit. Unde ipse ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. Et ipsum Christum Deus Pater dedit, id est constituit, caput, id est principalem, supra omnem Ecclesiam militantem ac triumphantem, quæ est corpus ipsius Christi mysticum, quoniam unitur ei ut capiti per communionem naturæ participationemque gratiæ. Est quoque Ecclesia plenitudo ejus, videlicet Christi, vel quia ab ipso donis gratiæ adimpletur, vel quia facit ad hoc, ut Christus omnia membra sua mystica habere dicatur, qui exsistens secundum divinitatis naturam, omnia in omnibus, non essentialiter aut formaliter, sed causaliter ac supereminenter, ut dictum est plenius, adimpletur, quantum ad mysticum corpus suum, quamvis in se ipso non perficiatur nec crescat.
paras.en: [[1:22|And he hath subjected all things under his feet|Et omnia subjecit sub pedibus ejus]][[Ps 8:8||]], that is, God the Father most fully subjected all created things to the power and command of Christ, and even to his lower nature (which may be understood by the name of *feet*). Hence he himself says: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]. [[1:22|and hath made him|Et ipsum]], Christ, God the Father *gave*, that is, appointed, [[1:22|head|caput]], that is, chief, [[1:22|over all the church|supra omnem Ecclesiam]], militant and triumphant, [[1:23|Which is his body|quæ est corpus ipsius]], the mystical body of Christ, since it is united to him as to its head by communion of nature and participation of grace. The Church is also [[1:23|the fulness of him|plenitudo ejus]] [the printed text omits *et*, “and”, restored in the margin], namely of Christ, either because it is filled by him with the gifts of grace, or because it brings it about that Christ is said to have all his mystical members, [[1:23|who|qui]], existing according to the nature of the Godhead, [[1:23|all in all|omnia in omnibus]], not essentially or formally but causally and supereminently, as has been said more fully, [[1:23|is filled|adimpletur]] as to his mystical body, though in himself he is neither perfected nor grows.

paras.t: Advertendum præterea, quod Christus dicitur caput Ecclesiæ, ad similitudinem capitis naturalis. Sicut enim in capite naturali sunt tria, videlicet: ordo, quoniam caput est prima atque superior pars hominis: perfectio, quia in capite vigent omnes sensus; virtus, quoniam motus et gubernatio omnium membrorum dependent a vi sensitiva ac motiva, quæ dominatur in capite: sic Christus prior et altior est aliis, propter gratiæ suæ eminentiam, et in ipso sunt omnes sensus spirituales, ipse quoque omnibus influere potest spiritualem sensum et gratiæ motum. Est autem Christus secundum utramque suam naturam caput totius Ecclesiæ; sed secundum divinam naturam, influit auctoritative, estque caput jure creationis atque excellentissimæ gubernationis. Secundum humanitatem vero, influit instrumentaliter: secundum quam etiam, Deus est caput Christi. — Nec hominum tantum, sed et angelorum quoque, Christus ut homo, caput censetur. Quemadmodum enim angelorum et hominum unus est ultimus finis atque felicitas, scilicet visio Dei per speciem, sic una est eorum Ecclesia. Multitudo namque electorum actibus officiisque distincta, mysticum Christi corpus vocatur. Quoniam igitur Christus, etiam ut homo, propter propinquitatem suam ad Verbum, influentiam habet in summos ordines angelorum et ceteros universos, eos purgando, illuminando et perficiendo, secundum magni Dionysii documenta: constat quod sit eorum caput Christus. Jam enim inductum est, quod Deus constituit eum super omnem principatum et potestatem, etc. Alibi quoque ab eodem Apostolo de ipso asseritur, quod est caput omnis principatus et potestatis.
paras.en: It is further to be noted that Christ is called head of the Church by likeness to a natural head. For as in a natural head there are three things, namely: order, since the head is the first and highest part of man; perfection, since all the senses flourish in the head; power, since the movement and governing of all the members depend on the sensitive and motive power that rules in the head: so Christ is prior to and higher than the others because of the eminence of his grace, and in him are all spiritual senses, and he can pour into all spiritual sense and the movement of grace. Christ is head of the whole Church according to both his natures; but according to the divine nature he pours in with authority, and is head by right of creation and of most excellent governance. According to his humanity he pours in instrumentally: according to which also [[1 Cor 11:3|the head of Christ is God|Deus est caput Christi]]. — And not of men only, but of angels too, Christ as man is reckoned head. For as angels and men have one last end and happiness, namely the vision of God face to face, so they have one Church. For the multitude of the elect, distinguished by acts and offices, is called the mystical body of Christ. Since, then, Christ, even as man, because of his nearness to the Word, has influence on the highest orders of angels and on all the rest, purging, illuminating and perfecting them, according to the teachings of the great Dionysius, it is clear that Christ is their head. For it has already been brought forward that God set him above all principality and power, etc. Elsewhere too the same Apostle asserts of him that he [[Col 2:10|is the head of all principality and power|est caput omnis principatus et potestatis]].

paras.t: Postremo sciendum, quod Christus est caput omnium, non æqualiter, sed ordine quodam. Primo enim et principaliter est caput Beatorum, qui ei uniuntur per gloriam fruitionis; secundo, eorum qui ei uniuntur per caritatem viæ; tertio autem, illorum qui sola fide ei junguntur; quarto vero, eorum qui uniuntur ei per potentiam ad actum reducendam; quinto (et maxime improprie), eorum qui uniuntur ei per potentiam nunquam ad actum reducendam. Damnatorum vero Christus caput non est; sed exsistentium in purgatorio caput veraciter appellatur.
paras.en: Lastly it is to be known that Christ is head of all, not equally, but in a certain order. First and chiefly he is head of the blessed, who are united to him by the glory of fruition; second, of those united to him by the charity of the way [that is, of this present life]; third, of those joined to him by faith alone; fourth, of those united to him in potency that will be brought to act; fifth (and most improperly), of those united to him in potency that will never be brought to act. Of the damned Christ is not the head; but of those in purgatory he is truly called the head.
